title: Through The Curtain Of His Body
subtitle: A torn curtain, all foods declared clean, a vision on a rooftop, and an inheritance that comes through a death
teaser: Jacob got his father's blessing by pretending to be the firstborn while his father was still alive. Hebrews says believers receive their inheritance a different way: the firstborn died, and his death secured the inheritance.
theme: At the cross the temple curtain was torn, the inheritance was secured through the Son’s death, and Gentiles were welcomed without becoming Jews; Christians still differ over whether Leviticus 11 binds their tables
framework: Hebrews 10:19-22 — the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body

modules.passage: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
emphasis: through the curtain of His body
modules.scriptureContext: Written to believers who knew the temple well. Only the high priest could pass the inner curtain, and only once a year.

modules.definition: covenant; also a last will and testament
modules.usage: The Greek Old Testament used this word for God's covenant with Israel. In everyday Greek it was also the normal word for a person's will. Hebrews 9:15 calls Christ “the mediator of a new covenant,” so that those who are called “may receive the promised eternal inheritance.” The next two verses speak of a diatheke taking effect only when the one who made it has died.
modules.usageNote: Translations divide on Hebrews 9:16-17. The Berean Standard Bible and the King James Version read “will” or “testament.” The New American Standard Bible reads “covenant.” Scholars divide the same way. Both readings join Christ's death to the inheritance in verse 15.

relatedWords.meaning: covenant, the Hebrew word diatheke translates

modules.heading: The Way In Is His Body
modules.content:
The first readers of Hebrews knew exactly what the curtain meant. It hung in front of the Most Holy Place. Behind it was the presence of God. Only the high priest went through it, only once a year, and only with blood.

That curtain was one of the clearest lessons of the law. God is holy, and people cannot walk into his presence as they are.

Hebrews says that has changed. Believers now have “confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus.” The way in is new and living, and it runs “through the curtain of His body.”

The writer does not say the curtain was unimportant. He says Christ's body became the way through it. What kept people out is now the way in, because Jesus gave his body in death.

So the invitation is plain. “Let us draw near.” The writer does not tell only the priests. He tells every believer. Come with a sincere heart and full assurance, with a conscience made clean.

The food laws marked Israel’s table, and the curtain marked access to the Most Holy Place. Hebrews says Christ’s death opened the way to God; Acts 10 says God welcomed Gentiles without treating them as unclean. Christians differ over what that welcome means for the Levitical food list.

modules.prompt: What keeps you standing outside the curtain when you have been invited in?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Jesus, the way to the Father runs through your body, given for me. I do not have to stand outside anymore. Give me the confidence Hebrews talks about, and let me draw near today with a clean conscience.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: the curtain torn from top to bottom, what Jesus said about food, Peter's vision, an inheritance that takes effect through a death, a priest who said “we lepers,” and the heel in Genesis 3:15.

modules.passage: But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last. And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
emphasis: the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom
modules.scriptureContext: Mark records the tearing at the moment of Jesus' death. The man who says “Truly this man was the Son of God” is a Roman soldier.

modules.heading: Torn From Top To Bottom
modules.content:
Mark tells the death of Jesus in very few words. Jesus cries out and dies. Then the veil of the temple is torn in two, from top to bottom.

Mark uses the Greek verb schizo, to tear, only twice in his whole Gospel. The first time is at Jesus' baptism, when the heavens are “breaking open” over him. The second is here. At the start of his ministry the heavens tear. At his death the curtain tears. Several scholars see the two moments as a deliberate pair, though that is an interpretation rather than something Mark states.

The temple had more than one curtain, and scholars disagree about which one Mark means. Some argue for the inner curtain in front of the Most Holy Place. Others argue for the outer curtain, which a centurion outside could have seen. The letter to the Hebrews clearly has the inner curtain in mind when it speaks of the way opened through Christ's body.

Readers also disagree about what the tearing means. Some see judgment on the temple. Some see open access to God. Some see the removal of the wall between peoples. These readings do not all exclude one another.

Mark gives the direction. It tears from top to bottom. No priest pulled it down from the floor. The tearing came from above.

C. H. Spurgeon preached on this in 1888.

“For believers the veil is not rolled up, but rent. The veil was not unhooked, and carefully folded up, and put away, so that it might be put in its place at some future time.”

The curtain was holy. God had commanded it. Hebrews reads the torn curtain as a way opened into God's presence.

modules.inlineImageAlt: An enormous woven temple curtain hanging from a high stone lintel, split cleanly from the top down to the floor, warm light falling through the gap onto the stone floor of an empty chamber
modules.inlineImageCaption: Torn from top to bottom. No priest pulled it down from the floor.

modules.passage: Once again Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “All of you, listen to Me and understand: Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.” After Jesus had left the crowd and gone into the house, His disciples inquired about the parable. “Are you still so dull?” He asked. “Do you not understand? Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him, because it does not enter his heart, but it goes into the stomach and then is eliminated.” (Thus all foods are clean.) He continued: “What comes out of a man, that is what defiles him. For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man.”
emphasis: Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him
modules.scriptureContext: The argument began when religious leaders saw Jesus' disciples eating with unwashed hands. Mark explains the custom to readers who did not know it.

modules.heading: What Goes Into A Man
modules.content:
The dispute in Mark 7 starts with hands, not animals. Some Pharisees see Jesus' disciples eating without the ritual washing their tradition required. Mark calls those hands “defiled,” and he explains to his readers that it means unwashed.

Jesus answers with a principle. Nothing entering a person from outside can defile him. What defiles a person comes from inside, from the heart. Then he lists the things that come out of a heart: evil thoughts, theft, greed, deceit, envy, slander, arrogance and more.

In the middle of that explanation, most modern translations print a short sentence in brackets. The Berean Standard Bible reads “(Thus all foods are clean.)” That sentence is Mark's comment, not a quotation of Jesus. It tells the reader what Mark understood Jesus' words to mean.

That reading goes back a long way. Origen and John Chrysostom, both writing before the year 400, read the words as Mark's explanation. Almost every modern translation follows them.

The King James Version reads differently. It says food “goeth out into the draught, purging all meats.” That translation follows a Greek text with a slightly different word form, and it makes the phrase describe digestion. In 2024 the New Testament scholar Logan Williams argued that the phrase really is part of Jesus' argument about digestion, not Mark's comment. His reading is a minority view, and it is taken seriously.

Christian traditions draw different conclusions from the passage. Catholic teaching says Jesus revealed the purpose of the food laws and declared all foods clean. Most Protestant traditions agree. Seventh-day Adventist scholars answer that Mark 7 concerns ritual hand-washing and human tradition, not the list in Leviticus 11. Some Messianic Jewish readers also take it that way.

Every one of these traditions accepts what Jesus says about the heart. A person can keep every rule about food and still be defiled by greed, envy and slander. A person can eat anything and still be defiled the same way.
Every one of these traditions accepts what Jesus says about the heart.

modules.passage: The next day at about the sixth hour, as the men were approaching the city on their journey, Peter went up on the roof to pray. He became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance. He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners. It contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air. Then a voice said to him: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” “No, Lord!” Peter answered. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.” The voice spoke to him a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” This happened three times, and all at once the sheet was taken back up into heaven.
emphasis: Do not call anything impure that God has made clean
modules.scriptureContext: Peter is in Joppa. Messengers from a Roman centurion named Cornelius are on their way to find him.
redLetter: Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.
Get up, Peter, kill and eat!

modules.heading: Not Any Man
modules.content:
Peter is hungry on a rooftop in Joppa when he sees the vision. A sheet comes down from heaven, full of animals Leviticus called unclean. A voice tells him to kill and eat.

Peter refuses. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.” He is being faithful to the law he grew up with. The Greek word he uses for unclean, akathartos, is the word the Greek Old Testament used for the Hebrew tamei in Leviticus.

The voice answers: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” It happens three times.

Then men arrive at the door, sent by Cornelius, a Roman centurion. Peter goes with them to a Gentile house. When he arrives, he tells the household what the vision meant.

“You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean.”

Peter applies the vision first to people. That is the one point every reading shares. Gordon Wenham, the evangelical scholar, argues that Acts 10 explicitly ties the welcome of Gentiles to the end of the food laws. Seventh-day Adventist writers answer that the vision was about people, as Peter's own explanation says, and they do not read it as permission to eat what Leviticus forbids. Both agree that God was opening his people to the nations.

Paul says the same thing about the cross in Ephesians 2. “For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility.” Christians read what follows in that passage in more than one way. Messianic Jewish writers hold that Jewish believers still keep the Torah as their calling. Every tradition agrees that Christ made Jews and Gentiles one people.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A man seen from behind kneeling on a flat whitewashed rooftop above a coastal town at midday, looking up as a great square linen sheet comes down out of a bright sky, held by its four corners
modules.inlineImageCaption: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” Peter first applied it to people.

modules.heading: Then and Now
modules.ancientTruth: In the first century, a Jew who ate at a Gentile's table crossed a real line. Peter says so in Cornelius's house. The temple curtain and the food laws both taught that nearness to God had conditions.
modules.modernApplication: Most churches today have forgotten how hard that line was to cross. We draw new lines instead. People are welcomed to God in principle and kept at a distance in practice, because of how they live, where they come from or what they eat.
modules.connectionPoint: In Acts 10 God did not call the old line foolish. He sent Peter, who had never eaten anything unclean, to a Gentile's house.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Peter summed it up afterward in Acts 15:9. God “made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.”

modules.passage: Therefore Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, now that He has died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant. In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it, because a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died; it cannot be executed while he is still alive.
emphasis: a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died
modules.scriptureContext: The Greek word for covenant in verse 15 is also the ordinary word for a will. Many scholars think Hebrews moves between the two senses here. Others hold that it means covenant throughout.

modules.heading: The Will Takes Effect
modules.content:
Hebrews 9 explains the inheritance with a word that had two meanings. Diatheke was the word for God's covenant, and it was also the word for a person's will. In verse 15 Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that the called “may receive the promised eternal inheritance.” Verses 16 and 17 then speak of a will that cannot take effect until the one who made it dies.

Translations and scholars divide here. Many translations read “will” in verses 16 and 17, including the Berean Standard Bible. The King James Version reads “testament.” Scholars such as F. F. Bruce and Harold Attridge agree. Others, including the New American Standard Bible and scholars such as Scott Hahn, argue that the author still means covenant. On their reading, the death is the penalty for a broken covenant, borne by Christ. Either way, verse 15 joins three things: Christ's death, the redemption of his people and the eternal inheritance.

John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage around the year 403, said this.

“We had offended: we ought to have died: He died for us and made us worthy of the Testament.”

Set that beside Jacob. Jacob received his father's blessing while his father was still alive, by pretending to be the firstborn. The blessing came through a lie, and it cost him twenty years away from home. The heirs in Hebrews receive their inheritance another way. The firstborn Son actually died, and his death put the inheritance into effect.

Many people speak of Christ's body as broken for us, and the King James Version reads “broken” in 1 Corinthians 11:24. The oldest manuscripts do not have that word, and most modern translations read “This is My body, which is for you.” John's Gospel is careful to say that not one of Jesus' bones was broken. What Jesus broke was the bread. Churches that say “broken for you” at the Lord's Table use the word for his wounding and death, not for his bones. Luke records his words at the table: “This is My body, given for you.”

So Scripture speaks of his body as given and slain. Hebrews says that through his body a new and living way has been opened through the curtain. Revelation 5 shows the Lamb in heaven, and the song there says, “You were slain.” Then the whole company of heaven sings.

“Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!”

The slain Lamb receives the blessing. In the same chapter he makes his people “a kingdom and priests.” The blessing comes to them through him, through the body that was given.

modules.inlineImageAlt: Looking straight down on a low wooden table at night, a round flat loaf torn into two pieces beside a clay cup of wine, lamplight at one corner, the edges of robed figures reclining around the table at the frame edge
modules.inlineImageCaption: What Jesus broke was the bread. “This is My body, given for you.”

modules.heading: We Lepers
modules.content:
In May 1873 a Belgian priest named Damien went to the settlement on the island of Molokai where the Hawaiian government sent people with leprosy. He later described what he found. Many patients lived in shelters made of branches and leaves. He himself was sheltered for several weeks under a single pandanus tree.

He stayed sixteen years. He dressed people's sores, washed their bodies, sat with them as they died and dug their graves. An English painter named Edward Clifford visited him in December 1888 and wrote down what he saw and heard.

By then Damien had the disease himself. It had been announced in 1884. Clifford recorded what Damien told him about his preaching.

“Whenever I preach to my people, I do not say ‘my brethren,’ as you do, but ‘we lepers.’”

Clifford made a sketch of him. When Damien looked at it, he said, “What an ugly face! I did not know the disease had made such progress.”

Damien died in April 1889. Soon after, a Protestant minister in Honolulu attacked him in a letter, calling him “a coarse, dirty man.” Robert Louis Stevenson, a Protestant who had visited the settlement after Damien's death, answered in print. He did not claim Damien was perfect. His own notes, gathered from people who had worked against the priest, called him stubborn, rough in his ways and careless about hygiene.

Then he wrote the sentence people remember.

“There is not a clean cup or towel in the Bishop-Home, but dirty Damien washed it.”
modules.connectionToTheme: Leviticus sent the person with a skin disease outside the camp. Damien went and lived inside that boundary until he could say “we.” That is a picture of what God did in Christ, not a proof of it.

modules.heading: Inside The Camp
modules.content:
Leviticus 13 gave a hard rule for a person with an infectious skin disease. He had to wear torn clothes and cover his mouth. He had to warn people away by crying out that he was unclean. The next sentence set the terms of his life while the disease lasted.

“He must live alone in a place outside the camp.”

The rule protected the camp, and it cost the sick person almost everything.

Mark 1 tells what Jesus did when such a man knelt in front of him. “Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man.” Then Jesus said, “I am willing. Be clean!” The man was cleansed.

The law kept such a man at a distance. In Mark's telling, Jesus closed the distance, and the man was made clean.

Damien's story echoes that, and it should not be pushed further than it goes. He had real faults, and Stevenson, who defended him, recorded them. What Damien shows is that a follower of Jesus could cross the line the law had drawn and stay with the people on the other side. The crossing itself belongs to Christ.

Hebrews 13 says Jesus “suffered outside the city gate” so that he could make his people holy by his own blood. The one who made people clean went outside the camp to do it.
modules.historicalContext: Edward Clifford, Father Damien: A Journey from Cashmere to His Home in Hawaii (Macmillan, 1889), chapter 3; Robert Louis Stevenson, Father Damien: An Open Letter to the Reverend Dr. Hyde of Honolulu (Sydney, 25 February 1890). Damien's birth, arrival and death dates follow the Vatican canonization biography (2009); Clifford gives his birth year wrongly. The popular story that Damien announced his illness in a single dramatic sermon beginning “we lepers” is not supported by the eyewitness record, which describes it as his habit. Leviticus 13:45-46 and Mark 1:40-42 are quoted from the Berean Standard Bible.

modules.inlineImageAlt: On a stony roadside, seen from behind a standing man in a woven mantle, a kneeling man in torn clothes with his hair hanging loose covers his mouth with one hand as the standing man's hand rests on his shoulder
modules.inlineImageCaption: The law sent him outside the camp. Jesus reached out his hand and touched him.

modules.passage: Then a leper came to Jesus, begging on his knees: “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed.
emphasis: Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man
modules.scriptureContext: Leviticus 13:46 required such a man to live outside the camp. He came to Jesus anyway, and Jesus touched him.

modules.prompt: Who have you kept outside the camp that Jesus would have touched?
additionalQuestions: Where do you still act as if you need to stand outside the curtain?
Which is harder for you to believe: that God opened the way to himself, or that he opened it to people you would rather keep at a distance?
What would it mean for you to receive an inheritance you did not earn and could not steal?

modules.heading: Do This With Your Body
modules.instruction: Today's is a physical practice. It takes about three minutes.

steps.description: Stand at the doorway of a room, just outside it.
Read Hebrews 10:19-20 aloud: since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body.
Notice that you have been standing outside. Stay there for a few breaths.
Then step through the doorway, slowly, and say: let us draw near.
Sit down inside the room for one minute. You were invited.

modules.passage: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”
modules.scriptureContext: God speaks to the serpent after the fall. Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, read this as the promise of Christ, born of a woman.

modules.heading: Holding On To The Heel That Was Struck
modules.content:
The first heel in the Bible is in Genesis 3:15. God tells the serpent that the woman's seed will crush its head, and that it will strike his heel.

Christians have read that verse as a promise of Christ for a very long time. Irenaeus, a bishop in Gaul around the year 180, wrote that the one born of a woman would keep watch for the serpent's head.

The Hebrew word for heel in Genesis 3:15 is aqev. It is the same word used when Jacob is born holding on to Esau's heel. The connection between those two verses is offered here as a reflection. We found no ancient Jewish or Christian writer who draws it, so hold it lightly.

Jacob held his brother's heel at birth. His early life was a contest for the birthright, the blessing and the firstborn's place.

The heel in Genesis 3 is different. It belongs to the one who is struck. The promised seed does not grab. He is wounded, and Christians read this as the serpent crushed through his wound.

A real find from Jerusalem shows how literal a struck heel could be. In 1968 archaeologists found the heel bone of a crucified man, still pierced by an iron nail 11.5 centimeters long, with olive wood under the nail's head. It shows that at least one man crucified in Roman Jerusalem was nailed through the heel. It does not tell us how Jesus was nailed, and it proves nothing about Genesis 3:15.

So a Christian comes to God like Jacob in one way. We come holding on to someone else's heel. We do not come to get ahead of him. We hold on because he was struck for us, and holding on to him is the only way in.

modules.inlineImageAlt: Wide view of a stony hill at the edge of a city wall under a pale sky, a single rough wooden cross standing on the rise, a small figure kneeling on the ground at a distance below it, seen from behind
modules.inlineImageCaption: The seed of the woman was struck. We come to God holding on to him.

modules.heading: Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord Jesus, you were struck so that the serpent would be crushed. Your body was given, and the curtain was torn from top to bottom. I have spent a lot of my life trying to get ahead of other people and trying to earn a place with God. Teach me to hold on to you instead. Let me come near with a clean conscience, and let me welcome the people you have made clean. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Breathe in: Your body, given for me. Breathe out: I draw near.

modules.heading: Carry This
modules.commitment: I will draw near to God through Christ, and I will stop calling unclean the people God has welcomed.
leavingAtCross: The belief that I must stay outside until I am good enough
The lines I draw to keep certain people away from God's table
receivingFromCross: A way in, opened through the body of Jesus
An inheritance that came through his death, not my disguise

modules.heading: Check Yourself
modules.question: What does the sentence “(Thus all foods are clean.)” in Mark 7:19 represent in most modern translations?
options: A later scribe's error that should be removed
Mark's own comment explaining what Jesus' words meant
A direct quotation of Jesus speaking to the Pharisees
A rule from Leviticus quoted by Jesus
modules.explanation: Most translations print the sentence as Mark's explanatory comment, a reading that goes back to Origen and Chrysostom. The King James Version follows a different Greek form and reads it as part of the description of digestion. A recent minority view reads it as part of Jesus' own argument.

modules.heading: The Priest Who Said We
modules.name: Father Damien of Molokai
modules.bio: Jozef De Veuster, a Belgian priest, arrived at the leprosy settlement on Molokai in May 1873 and stayed until his death in April 1889. He contracted the disease and was known for dressing wounds and digging graves. His defender Robert Louis Stevenson recorded his faults as honestly as his courage.
modules.keyQuote: Whenever I preach to my people, I do not say ‘my brethren,’ as you do, but ‘we lepers.’
modules.lessonForUs: He crossed a line the world drew around the sick and stayed on the other side of it. He did not pretend to be a better man than he was.

modules.forDeeperStudy: Sources for today. Diatheke is G1242; katapetasma G2665; schizo G4977, in Mark only at 1:10 and 15:38. On which curtain tore and what it meant: Daniel M. Gurtner, “The Rending of the Veil,” Themelios 29.3. Mark 7:19: Bruce Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament; Logan Williams, “The Stomach Purifies All Foods,” New Testament Studies 70 (2024); Catechism of the Catholic Church 582; David Merling, “Clean and unclean meat,” Ministry (June 1999). Acts 10: Gordon Wenham, Evangelical Quarterly 53 (1981). Hebrews 9:16-17: Jared Compton's 2025 survey names Attridge, Bruce, Koester and Schreiner for “will,” and Hughes, Hahn, Jamieson and others for “covenant.” Chrysostom, Homily 16 on Hebrews, section 2. 1 Corinthians 11:24: “broken” is absent from the oldest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus first hand, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and from modern critical editions; John 19:36. Spurgeon, “The Rent Veil,” Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit No. 2015 (1888). Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.21.1. The same Hebrew noun aqev (H6119) appears in Genesis 3:15 and 25:26; no traditional source linking the two was found. The Giv'at ha-Mivtar heel bone: Joseph Zias and Eliezer Sekeles, Israel Exploration Journal 35 (1985), which corrected earlier reports. Damien: Edward Clifford (1889) and Robert Louis Stevenson (1890).
